232.title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (1 of 7)
232.hook: a new camp opens with a text so short it fits on one page
232.tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (2 of 7)
232.howItsDone: Many Hindus know the Isha Upanishad's first verse by heart, and it is often chanted along with the 'purnam adah' peace invocation that traditionally opens the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita closed: eighteen chapters, and your line was you actually read it. Today the path goes underneath it.

Eighteen verses. It fits on one page, and people have written whole books about its first line. It's one of the Upanishads, the older texts underneath the Gita, the ones it draws on: the Gita quotes them, borrows their pictures, sometimes their exact verses. Many texts carry the name, and tradition sets apart a small group as the principal ones. Camp five, the depths, spends a week each on four of them, starting with one of the shortest.
screen: `EIGHTEEN VERSES.` → `UNDERNEATH THE GITA.` → `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.`

segments.voice: The word Upanishad is usually explained as sitting down near: upa, near, ni, down, shad, to sit. A student sitting close to a teacher, close enough to hear something said quietly. That's the feel of these texts. Not a law code, not a hymnbook. A conversation near the fire. The Isha Upanishad is named after its first word. Isha means the Lord, the one who rules. The verse opens: isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is vasyam by the Lord. That one word, vasyam, can be read two ways. Some commentators read it as dwelt in, pervaded: the Lord lives inside everything, the way salt lives in seawater. The great teacher Shankara read it as covered, clothed: wrap everything you see in the thought of the Lord, the way you'd wrap a gift. Either way, the claim is enormous. Not some things. All this. The coffee cup. The traffic. The person you find difficult. The second half of the verse is where this week's word comes from, and it's tomorrow's lesson. But hold the first half for a day, because everything else in the Upanishad leans on it. If all this belongs to the Lord, then nothing here is only mine. And nothing here is only ordinary. Mahatma Gandhi is often quoted as saying that if all the other scriptures were lost and only this first verse remained, Hinduism would live on. That's a lot of weight for one line. This week will show whether it can carry it.
screen: `UPANISHAD: SITTING DOWN NEAR.` · `ISHA: THE LORD.` · `DWELT IN, OR CLOTHED.` · `NOT SOME THINGS. ALL THIS.` · then, large: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of you, a wall, a window, your own hands, and try the verse on it: all this; whatever your tradition calls the sacred, or simply life itself, imagine it living inside the thing you're looking at. Then close your eyes and try it on the sounds around you, then on your own breath. If you pray, you can say the two words isha vasyam quietly; if not, just notice.
Isha, the Lord, the one who rules. Today, the first half of the Isha's first verse: all this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Tomorrow, the renouncing and the enjoying.
Your line: nothing here is only mine. For today, just the ground under it. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (2 of 7)
233.hook: the second half of the first verse, and a question: whose is it?
233.carry: let them go when they go
233.tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (3 of 7)
233.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers read 'tena tyaktena bhunjitha' as a rule for householders: live fully in the world, holding possessions as a trust rather than as one's own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, isha: the first half of the first verse. All this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Nothing here is only mine.
screen: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: A book lent to a friend can do something odd. While it's gone, its owner may think about it more than when it sat on the shelf. When it comes back, it gets noticed again. That's the strange thing about holding: the tighter the grip, the less there is to taste. A hand busy guarding can't do much else. The second half of the Isha's first verse turns on exactly this. Three short phrases: one instruction, one warning, and a question that sounds almost rude.
screen: `THE BOOK LENT TO A FRIEND.` → `GUARDING IS NOT TASTING.` → `THE SECOND HALF.`

segments.voice: Here's the second half. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Or, as it's often put, enjoy through renunciation. Tyakta is let go, given up. Bhunjitha is enjoy, eat, have the use of. They sit side by side, and that's the surprise. You might expect a holy text to say: renounce, so you won't enjoy. This one says letting go is how you get to enjoy. Why? Go back to yesterday. If all this belongs to the Lord, you were never the owner. You're a guest at a table someone else set. A guest who grabs the dishes and hides them under the chair doesn't enjoy dinner. A guest who knows it's all a gift can eat with both hands. Next comes the warning: ma gridhah. Do not covet. Don't grasp at more. Then the question: kasya svid dhanam? Whose, indeed, is wealth? Commentators read it two ways. Don't covet anyone's wealth, because it isn't really theirs either. Or, more pointed: whose is it, really? The verse has already answered: the Lord's. Renouncing here doesn't have to mean leaving home or giving everything away, though some in the tradition do exactly that. For a householder, some teachers, Gandhi among them, say it means holding things as a trustee, not a proprietor. Use them. Love them. Let them go when they go.
screen: `BY THAT RENOUNCED, ENJOY.` · `A GUEST AT A TABLE SET BY ANOTHER.` · `DO NOT COVET.` · `WHOSE IS WEALTH?` · then, large: `RENOUNCE AND ENJOY.`

segments.voice: Hold something in your hand, a phone, a cup, a pen, feel its weight, and say to yourself: not mine, lent; notice whether it feels any different. Then set it down, rest your open hands on your knees, and let each breath be something received and given back: in, received; out, returned.
Tyaktena, by what is let go. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Don't covet. Whose is wealth?
Your line: let them go when they go. A guest at the table never owned the dishes. See you tomorrow.

234.title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (3 of 7)
234.hook: a text about letting go that tells you to live a hundred years, working
234.tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (4 of 7)
234.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Isha verse 2 to show that the Upanishads do not require leaving the world: a householder can work a full life without being bound by the work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tyaktena: by that renounced, enjoy. Do not covet; whose is wealth? Your line: let them go when they go.

Why not just quit? If everything belongs to the Lord, and the wise thing is to let go, why not leave the job, leave the inbox, and go sit under a tree? Some in the tradition have done exactly that, and they're honored for it. But the very next verse of the Isha says something closer to the opposite. It's the verse that makes this tiny Upanishad a favorite of people with rent to pay.
screen: `WHY NOT JUST QUIT?` → `THE NEXT VERSE.` → `NOT THE ANSWER YOU EXPECT.`

segments.voice: Verse two: kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah. Doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years. Karmani is works, actions, the same karma you learned on day seven: action, and what it grows. Shatam samah, a hundred years, is the full human life in the old Vedic hope. So the text that just said let go now says: live long, and keep working. Then the reason. For you, living this way, there is no other way; action does not cling to a person. The word for cling pictures something smeared on, like oil or mud. Actions done in the spirit of verse one, knowing all this belongs to the Lord, don't glue themselves to you. That's the seed of the Gita's karma yoga, which you spent weeks with: act fully, and don't cling to the fruit. Here it is centuries earlier, in two lines. Verse three is darker. It speaks of worlds called asurya, covered in blind darkness, where those who are killers of the self go. Some translators hear asurya as sunless; others, Shankara among them, as the worlds of the asuras. Either way, it's dark. Most commentators don't read killers of the self as literal suicide, but as people who live as if the self weren't there at all, burying the light under grabbing. So the three verses stack up. All this is the Lord's. Enjoy it by letting go. And keep working, a hundred years if you get them, without letting the work stick. Renounce, and enjoy, and get up tomorrow.
screen: `DOING WORKS HERE.` · `LIVE A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `ACTION DOES NOT CLING.` · `THE WORLDS OF BLIND DARKNESS.` · then, large: `RENOUNCE, AND KEEP WORKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary task waiting for you, a report, the dishes, a phone call, and see yourself doing it well, then finishing it and letting it go, the way you'd wash oil off your hands. Breathe in as you picture the work; breathe out as you picture it done and released. If your mind runs to the result, how it'll be judged, notice that, and come back to the doing.
Karma, action, works. Verse two adds: and keep working. Doing works here, wish to live a hundred years; action done this way doesn't cling.
Your line: don't let the work stick. Work done this way doesn't follow you to dinner. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

235.title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (4 of 7)
235.hook: it moves and it does not move; it is far, and it is near
235.tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (5 of 7)
235.howItsDone: Isha verse 5, 'tad ejati tan naijati', is chanted in Vedic recitation and quoted in Hindu teaching to show that the divine is both beyond the world and within it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma: doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years, and the action doesn't cling. Your line: don't let the work stick.

Try describing the sky to someone. It's up there. But it's also right here, touching your face; you're breathing it. It's the biggest thing you'll ever see, and you can't hold a piece of it. Every sentence you make about it is true and a little wrong. Verses four and five of the Isha try to describe the one who pervades all this. Instead of a definition, they give a string of contradictions. On purpose.
screen: `DESCRIBE THE SKY.` → `TRUE, AND A LITTLE WRONG.` → `A STRING OF CONTRADICTIONS.`

segments.voice: Verse four: it is one, unmoving, and swifter than the mind. The senses can't catch it; it's always ahead of them. Standing still, it outruns those who run. Then verse five: tad ejati tan naijati. It moves; it does not move. Tad dure tad v antike. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and outside all this. Why talk like this? Because any single statement would shrink it. Say it's far away, in heaven, and you've made it absent from your kitchen. Say it's right here, and you've made it small enough to fit in a room. The Upanishad holds both at once, like two ends of a rope pulled taut. You met the same move in the Gita, where Krishna says everything rests in him and also that he isn't contained by any of it. Later schools of Hindu thought read these verses differently. Those who follow Shankara's Advaita, non-duality, hear the one reality behind every appearance. Those who follow Ramanuja hear a personal Lord who lives in everything as its inner self, while still being more than it. Both are reading the same two lines. And notice where this sits: right after the verses about living and working in the world. The one you're looking for isn't only at the end of a long journey. It's also near, nearer than the next thought. Swifter than the mind, and still.
screen: `SWIFTER THAN THE MIND.` · `IT MOVES; IT DOES NOT MOVE.` · `FAR, AND NEAR.` · `INSIDE ALL THIS, AND OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `TAD DURE TAD V ANTIKE.`

segments.voice: Sit very still and notice that something still moves: the breath, the heartbeat, a passing thought. Then notice something far away, a sound outside or someone in another city, and something near, the air on your skin. Let the verse sit with you, it moves, it does not move, far and near; you don't have to understand it, just notice both.
Ejati, it moves, it stirs. Tad ejati tan naijati: it moves, it does not move; it is far, and it is near, inside all this and outside it.
Your line: nearer than the next thought. Far, and near, at once. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (5 of 7)
236.hook: whoever sees all beings in the self no longer shrinks from anyone
236.tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (6 of 7)
236.howItsDone: Isha verses 6 and 7 are often quoted by Hindu teachers, especially in the Vedanta traditions, as the root of seeing the one self in every being.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ejati: it moves and does not move, far and near, inside all this and outside it. Your line: nearer than the next thought.

A man on the train is talking to himself, loudly. A relative starts in on politics at dinner. A bad photo of your own face turns up. Something in the body pulls back, a small recoil, before a single thought has formed. Verses six and seven of the Isha are about that flinch. They say there's a way of seeing that makes it go away. Not by trying harder to be nice. By seeing differently.
screen: `THE FLINCH.` → `A SMALL RECOIL.` → `A WAY OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Verse six: the one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not shrink away from anything. The verb is vijugupsate: to recoil, to feel aversion, to shrink back in disgust. That's the flinch, named. And the cure isn't a rule. It's a seeing. If the same self is in you and in the man on the train, pulling away from him is a bit like pulling away from your own hand. Verse seven goes further. For the one who sees oneness, ekatvam, what delusion is there, what sorrow? It's phrased as a question, the way verse one ended. Not no sorrow ever, but: where would sorrow get a grip? Verse eight then describes the one who pervades all this, in a lovely list. Bright. Bodiless. Without wound. Pure. Untouched by evil. The seer, the wise one, the one who is everywhere, self-existent, who has set things in order for all time. See how it ties the week together. On day one, all this is pervaded by the Lord. Here, you see the same in every being. On this reading, renouncing isn't only letting go of things. It's letting go of the wall between you and everyone else. And enjoying becomes bigger: not just enjoying your coffee, but not having to flinch. You met this in the Gita too, where the sage sees the same in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the one who eats dogs. The Isha puts it in two lines.
screen: `ALL BEINGS IN THE SELF.` · `NO LONGER SHRINKING BACK.` · `WHAT SORROW, FOR ONE WHO SEES ONENESS?` · `BRIGHT, BODILESS, PURE.` · then, large: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone mildly difficult, not the hardest person in your life, notice the small recoil in your body, the jaw, the shoulders, and breathe into it. Then try the verse as an experiment: the same life that's breathing in you is breathing in them. See if the flinch softens, even slightly; if it doesn't, that's fine, you looked.
Ekatva, oneness. For the one who sees oneness, what delusion is there, what sorrow? See all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, and stop shrinking back.
Your line: stop shrinking back. The same self is in you and in the one you flinch from. Until tomorrow.

237.title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (6 of 7)
237.hook: into blind darkness go those who follow ignorance, and into greater darkness those who follow knowledge alone
237.tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (7 of 7)
237.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of different schools read Isha verses 9–14 differently, but the verses are commonly taught as a call to hold inner knowledge and outer action together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekatva, oneness. The one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, stops shrinking back.

Two kinds of people can be hard to be around. One only cares about practical things: money, the schedule, what's for dinner, and never asks why. The other only cares about ideas: always reading, always explaining, and somehow never takes out the trash. Verses nine to fourteen of the Isha sound strange at first. They warn against something like both. And the warning for the second kind is harsher.
screen: `ONLY THE PRACTICAL.` → `ONLY THE IDEAS.` → `A WARNING FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Verse nine: into blind darkness enter those who follow avidya, not-knowing. Into a greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in vidya, knowing, alone. Knowledge, on its own, gets the worse darkness. What do the two words mean here? Vidya is knowledge, but Shankara takes it here as knowledge of the gods: meditation, inner study. Avidya, on his reading, is ritual action, work in the world, the practical side. Other teachers read the pair differently, and scholars still argue. The text itself doesn't define them. But it does say what to do with them. Verse eleven: the one who knows both together crosses death by avidya and gains the deathless by vidya. Not one or the other. Both, together. Verses twelve to fourteen run the same pattern with another pair: the manifest and the unmanifest, becoming and non-becoming. Again, those who follow only one go into darkness, and knowing both together is the way through. It fits the week. Verse two said keep working a hundred years. Verses six and seven spoke of seeing the one self. Here the Isha won't let you pick. Contemplation without action floats away. Action without contemplation gets lost. Renounce and enjoy has the same shape: two things that sound opposite, held in one hand. Doing the dishes and asking why you're alive belong in the same day.

238.howItsDone: Isha verses 15–18 are recited at some Hindu funerals and at the bedside of the dying; verse 18, the prayer to Agni to lead by the good path, also appears in the Rig Veda (1.189.1).

segments.voice: Yesterday, vidya: know both together, knowing and doing, vidya and avidya. Either alone goes dark.

Some things that get in the way of seeing clearly are ugly. But the hardest ones to see past are beautiful. A great job that's slowly emptying you. Praise that feels so good you stop asking whether it's deserved. A shiny screen at midnight. The Isha ends with a picture of exactly this. Not truth hidden behind a wall, or a curtain, or a mess. Truth hidden behind gold. And then the text does something it hasn't done all week. It prays.
screen: `THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS IN THE WAY.` → `NOT A WALL.` → `GOLD.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen: hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc, or a golden vessel, like a lid. The speaker turns to Pushan, the nourisher, a name for the sun: uncover it, so that I, whose way is truth, may see. Verse sixteen goes on: spread out your rays, gather in your light, so I can see your most blessed form. Then a startling line: that person there, I am he. The one hidden behind the gold is not a stranger. Verse seventeen is spoken at the edge of death: the breath goes back to the immortal wind, and this body ends in ashes. Then: om, mind, remember. Remember what was done. And verse eighteen, the last, turns to Agni, fire: lead us by the good path, you who know all our ways; take away from us the crooked wrong. Tradition gives these verses a place at deathbeds and funerals, and they read that way: close, and quiet. They aren't a new teaching. They're the whole week turned into a prayer. So, the week. All this is pervaded by the Lord. By that renounced, enjoy. Keep working a hundred years, and the work won't cling. It moves and doesn't move, far and near. See the self in all beings and stop shrinking back. Hold knowing and doing together. And when even the good things shine too brightly, ask for the gold to be moved aside. Eighteen verses, isha: nothing here is only mine.
screen: `THE FACE OF TRUTH, COVERED WITH GOLD.` · `UNCOVER IT, SO I MAY SEE.` · `MIND, REMEMBER.` · `LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.` · then, large: `ISHA.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what the golden lid in your life is right now: something good, even lovely, that might be keeping you from seeing what's true; you don't have to remove it, just name it quietly. Then breathe, and on each out-breath imagine the lid lifting a little. If you pray, you can say the verse's own request in your own language, uncover it, so I may see; otherwise, just watch the breath.
Hiranmaya, golden, made of gold. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc; Pushan, the sun, is asked to uncover it, so the truthful may see.
Your line: uncover it, so I may see. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad that starts with a child's question. That's the whole Isha, and day two hundred thirty-eight.
